title: Check yourself: primitive types at their edges

questions.stem: A disk report computes `long usedBytes = blocks * 4096;`, where `blocks` is an `int`. A volume has 600,000 blocks in use. What does `usedBytes` hold, and why?

options.text: 2,457,600,000, since the receiving variable is a `long`, so the `int` operands are multiplied in 64 bits
options.says: an expression's type comes from its operands, not from the variable that receives it

options.text: A negative number, since both operands are `int`, so the product wraps before the `long` receives it
options.says: 2,457,600,000 is above Integer.MAX_VALUE; the int product wraps and the long receives the wrapped value

options.text: 2,457,600,000, since an `int` product that does not fit is widened, so the `long` receives every bit
options.says: nothing widens on overflow: the high bits are dropped

options.text: Nothing, since an `int` product past its range throws, so the `long` is never assigned
options.says: plain int arithmetic wraps without an error; it is Math.multiplyExact and Math.addExact that throw instead

origin.section: Integer Arithmetic Wraps Without an Error, Even When the Result Goes Into a long

questions.stem: Two services compute the same yearly revenue as a `double`, about 4e10, and their results differ only in the last binary digit. A reconciliation job reports them as equal when `Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9`. What does it report?

options.text: Equal, since 1e-9 is a tolerance, so a last-digit difference falls inside it
options.says: a fixed tolerance stops working as values grow: near 4e10 a last-digit difference is far above 1e-9

options.text: Different, since subtracting two doubles that close gives `NaN`, so the test is `false`
options.says: the difference is a small ordinary number; NaN comes from operations such as 0.0 / 0

options.text: Different, since a last-digit difference at that size is above 1e-9, so the test is `false`
options.says: doubles are spaced by their size; near 1e9 the spacing is already 1.19e-7, so at 4e10 a tolerance of 1e-9 is just ==

options.text: Equal, since a last-digit difference at that size is below 1e-9, so the test is `true`
options.says: the size of the last binary digit grows with the value; at 1e9 it is already 1.19e-7

origin.section: A double Holds a Binary Fraction, So Compare Computed Values With a Tolerance That Fits Their Size

questions.stem: A health job runs `double avg = (double) totalMs / samples;` and then `if (avg > 250.0) page(); else markHealthy();`. Both are `long`s, and in a quiet hour both are 0. What happens?

options.text: It throws `ArithmeticException`, since dividing by zero is an error for every numeric type
options.says: only integer division by zero throws; floating-point division returns Infinity or NaN

options.text: It calls `page()`, since `avg` is `Infinity`, which is above 250.0
options.says: 0.0 / 0 is NaN; it is 1.0 / 0 that is Infinity

options.text: It throws `ArithmeticException`, since the cast applies after the two `long`s are divided
options.says: the page's (double) failed / requests on two zero longs returns NaN instead of throwing; only the division on the longs themselves throws

options.text: It calls `markHealthy()`, since `avg` is `NaN`, which fails the `>` test
options.says: 0.0 / 0 is NaN, every comparison with NaN is false, so the else branch runs

origin.section: Integer Division by Zero Throws; Floating-Point Division Returns Infinity or NaN, and NaN Equals Nothing

questions.stem: An order service checks `order.quantity() == stock.reserved()`, where both return an `Integer` boxed from an `int` parsed out of request text. On a JVM with default settings, an order for 300 meets 300 reserved units. What does the check give?

options.text: `true`, since `==` unboxes both `Integer` operands, so it compares the two values
options.says: == on two wrappers compares references, not values

options.text: `false`, since `==` compares the two references, so the two 300s are different objects
options.says: == on two wrappers compares references; Integer.valueOf, which autoboxing calls, always caches only -128 to 127, and 128 == 128 already printed false

options.text: `true`, since boxing reuses one object per value, so the two 300s are one object
options.says: the cache always covers -128 to 127 and only may cover more; 128 == 128 printed false, so equal values above 127 can be two objects

options.text: `false`, since `==` compares the two hash codes, so the two 300s hash differently
options.says: == on two wrappers compares references, not hash codes

origin.section: A Wrapper Is an Object: It Can Be null, and == Compares References
